contention_points.description: Both sides agree that plastic ocean pollution is harmful.
Both sides agree that consumer convenience matters.
Both sides agree that economic harm to low-income communities should be avoided.
Side A says bans reduce plastic waste; side B says bans just shift to alternatives with higher lifecycle emissions. This is a factual question with measurable answers.
Side A prioritizes ecosystem protection over short-term economic cost; side B prioritizes economic freedom over regulatory intervention. Neither side can be settled by evidence alone.
Side A argues a ban is the most effective policy lever; side B argues market incentives (taxes) work better. This is an empirical question about policy effectiveness.
Side A says bans are justified by externalities; side B says externalities should be priced in, not banned. This is a fundamental difference in the appropriate role of government.
Side A says 'single-use plastics' means items used once and discarded; side B thinks the debate is about 'all plastic packaging including compostable'. They are answering different questions.
Side A says the alternatives are 'sustainable'; side B says they're worse lifecycle-wise. 'Sustainable' means different things to each side (carbon vs. marine litter).
Side A claims bans 'work' citing reduced beach litter; side B claims bans 'don't work' citing unchanged total plastic production. They are measuring different outcomes.
Whether reduced plastic litter translates to measurable marine biodiversity improvement is an open empirical question.
Whether the burden of cost falls disproportionately on low-income households is an empirical distributional question.
Both sides agree that corporate accountability for waste is desirable in principle.
